title: Noise-limited secret key agreement with twin optical physically unclonable functions
abstract: We investigate the use of twin optical fingerprints derived from correlated physical unclonable functions (PUFs), as a hardware-based platform for cryptographic key generation and distribution. Each fingerprint is associated with a random, yet reproducible speckle pattern, generated when coherent light is scattered by a disordered optical structure. We consider a pair of correlated optical PUFs, and study the conditions under which two honest parties can establish a common secret key, despite fabrication-induced variability and environmental noise. An explicit information-theoretic key-agreement protocol is developed, incorporating secure sketches, error reconciliation, and privacy amplification. We quantify information leakage due to public helper data, and derive lower bounds on the length of the final secret key. The analysis identifies the noise regimes in which secure key agreement is feasible, and examines the performance of both practical and near-capacity reconciliation schemes. Finally, we discuss how twin optical PUFs could be integrated into quantum key distribution (QKD) networks, as a mechanism for establishing an initial pre-shared secret key between two honest users, without relying on computational assumptions or trusted third parties.
summary: This paper proposes using twin optical PUFs as a physical source for establishing secret keys between two parties. It develops an explicit, information-theoretic key-agreement protocol that accounts for noise and fabrication imperfections. The work demonstrates how this hardware platform can securely generate pre-shared keys, potentially seeding Quantum Key Distribution networks without relying on computational assumptions.
main_problem: To develop an information-theoretic protocol for establishing a shared secret key using twin optical Physical Unclonable Functions (PUFs) that is robust against noise and environmental variability.
main_result: The authors developed a general, explicit key-agreement protocol incorporating secure sketches, error reconciliation, and privacy amplification, showing feasibility in specific noise regimes.
method: The methodology involves modeling the PUF response using correlated optical scattering matrices and applying established cryptographic techniques (error correction codes) to distill a secret key from noisy raw measurements.
model_or_system: The physical platform is based on twin Optical PUFs, where fingerprints are derived from speckle patterns generated by coherent light scattering through disordered optical structures. The underlying model uses transmission matrices whose elements are treated as complex Gaussian random variables.
key_observables: Speckle pattern intensity, final secret key length (lower bound), and the disagreement probability (Bit-Error Rate).
important_parameters: Fabrication variability ($\sigma_F$), environmental noise ($\sigma_E$), and the maximum allowed Hamming distance ($t$).
main_assumptions: The protocol assumes that the challenge conveys no information about the PUF output, and it is designed to function without relying on computational assumptions or trusted third parties.
figures_summary: Figure 1 schematically illustrates the main steps in key agreement using twin PUFs, detailing the flow from raw measurements through reconciliation to the final shared secret key.
paper_structure: The paper first models the optical PUF response mathematically, then develops an information-theoretic protocol incorporating error correction and privacy amplification. It analyzes the security bounds based on noise parameters and concludes by discussing integration into QKD networks.
why_interesting: This work bridges quantum optics (light scattering in disordered media) with quantum information theory by proposing a hardware-based method for generating cryptographic keys, which is highly relevant to quantum networking infrastructure.
